title: Design a payment system
dek: A customer pays ₹480 for an order by UPI or card, through a payment gateway. Charge them exactly once, never tell them "failed" when the money actually went, and keep books that match the bank's to the paisa.

items: You don't move the money yourself: a payment gateway talks to UPI and the card networks. Your job is to ask once, track the answer, and keep correct books.

One payment per order attempt, with the order as its idempotency key on your API, and passed to the gateway as your reference. A double tap or a retry finds the same payment instead of making a second.
A timeout doesn't mean failed. Mark it unknown, ask the gateway until it settles, and never invite the person to pay again while it's unknown.
Record every money movement as entries in a ledger that are only ever added, never edited, and that always balance.
Every day, match the gateway's settlement report against your ledger. Anything that doesn't match goes to a person, not a script.
Pay for an order by UPI or card; the order is confirmed only when the payment has succeeded.
Never charge a customer twice for one order, whatever they tap or the network does.
Refunds, full or part, when an order is cancelled or something is missing.
Books that say exactly who owes whom, and match the gateway's reports.
Out of scope here: paying restaurants and riders (payouts), wallets, and fraud scoring, which we'll note where it plugs in.

body.label: Qualities to aim for
head: Quality
Target
rows: No double charges; every rupee in the ledger matches the gateway
The customer always sees one of paid, failed, or "checking, don't pay again"
Checkout works even if one gateway is down (a second gateway)
1 crore orders a day, about 500 payments a second at dinner

items: 1 crore orders a day is about 115 payments a second on average; dinner is about four times that, so plan for 500.
That's small for a database. The hard parts are correctness and talking to slow outside systems, not volume.
Each payment adds 2 to 4 ledger entries, so 2 to 4 crore rows a day, about 10 GB a day at 300 bytes a row. Keep it all; books are kept for years.
UPI approvals usually take seconds, but a few percent take longer or time out. At 500 a second, that's several unknown payments every second that need to be settled.
Payment: `id`, `order_id`, `idempotency_key`, `amount` (in paise, an integer), `method`, `gateway`, `gateway_ref`, `status` (created, pending, succeeded, failed, unknown, refunded), `updated_at`.
Ledger entry: `id`, `payment_id`, `account` (customer, Zotato's gateway receivable, restaurant payable…), `debit` or `credit`, `amount`, `at`. Entries for one movement always balance.
Refund: `id`, `payment_id`, `amount`, `status`, `gateway_ref`.
Webhook log: every message from the gateway, as received, with its signature check result.

body.label: API
body.say: Create a payment for an order (the same key returns the same payment). Ask its status. Ask for a refund, also with a key.

body.x: The amount comes from the order service, never from the app. An app can be changed to send ₹1.

body.cap: The payment service creates the payment, with the order as its key, and hands the app to the gateway. The gateway's result comes back as a signed webhook; it's recorded in the ledger and passed to the order service. The app asks us whether it's paid, not the gateway.

body.x: Only the payment service talks to gateways. Everything else asks it. That keeps one place that knows the truth about each payment, and one place to add a second gateway.

body.name: First try
body.what: Grey out the button after the first tap and hope for the best.
body.avoid: It does nothing for a retry after a network error, a second phone, or the app being reopened. Each of those creates a new charge.
body.ex: Ananya's 4G drops after she approves in her UPI app. The app retries, a second request shows up in her UPI app, she approves it thinking the first failed, and pays ₹960.
body.like: Telling a cashier "I've already paid" with no receipt.

body.name: Better
body.kind: ONE PAYMENT PER ORDER ATTEMPT, BY KEY
body.what: The idempotency key is the order (and attempt number). Creating a payment with a key that exists returns the existing payment. Send your order id to the gateway as its merchant reference (and an idempotency key where the gateway offers one), and look it up there before any retry.
body.use: Any number of retries, from any device, lead to one payment and at most one charge.
body.avoid: A real second attempt (the first failed) needs a new attempt number, and only after the first is known to have failed.
body.ex: The retry for order #91 finds pay_3, already pending, and simply shows its status.
body.like: A token number at the counter: asking again just gets you the same token.

body.cap: Created, pending while the person approves in their UPI app, then succeeded or failed. A timeout makes it unknown: keep asking the gateway until it settles. Never show "failed" for an unknown payment, or the person pays again.

items: When the gateway doesn't answer in time, mark the payment unknown and tell the person "Checking with your bank. Don't pay again."
Settle it two ways: the gateway's webhook, and your own status checks every few seconds, then minutes. Whichever arrives first wins; the second is a no-op.
A success that arrives late, after the order was already cancelled, is refunded automatically. That's normal, not a bug.

Never keep a balance you change in place. Record each movement as ledger entries that are only added: a ₹480 debit to "gateway owes Zotato" and a matching ₹480 credit to order #91's account. A refund is new entries the other way, not an edit.
Entries for one movement always balance: debits equal credits. A daily check that the whole ledger balances catches bugs early.
Store amounts as whole paise, never as decimals, so ₹480.10 never turns into ₹480.0999.

Reconcile every day: the gateway's settlement report lists what it collected, its fee and GST, and what it paid into Zotato's bank. Match it to the ledger, payment by payment. Mismatches go to a queue for a person.
Check the signature on every webhook, and look the payment up by its gateway reference, never trust the amount in the message alone.
Webhooks come late, twice and out of order. Save each one, answer quickly, and process it from the saved copy; moving from succeeded back to pending is ignored.
Never see or store card numbers: the gateway's page or SDK collects them and a saved card is kept as a network token, as RBI's card-on-file rules require. That keeps most of PCI DSS off your servers.
A second gateway: if one is failing, new payments go to the other. A payment always stays with the gateway it started on.
Junior / mid: a payment service in front of a gateway, payment statuses, webhooks, refunds.
Senior: idempotency keys end to end, unknown versus failed, late successes, server-side amounts, an append-only ledger.
Lead: double-entry books and daily reconciliation, webhook signatures and ordering, a second gateway, paise not decimals, where fraud checks and payouts plug in.
"Pay restaurants every day?" A payout job that reads the ledger's restaurant payable balances, sends transfers with their own idempotency keys, and records them as entries.
"Part refunds?" A refund with an amount, never more than what's left of the payment, checked in the same transaction that records it.
"The ledger table gets huge?" It's append-only, so split by month; old months are read-only and easy to archive.
"Fraud?" A risk check before creating the payment (new device, many failed attempts, unusual amount) that can ask for extra verification.
"How do you test it?" A fake gateway that times out, answers twice, sends webhooks out of order and lies in its reports; then check the ledger and reconciliation catch every case.

body.x: Like a payment, a saved order is a promise: it must not vanish when a part crashes. The lost-orders challenge practises keeping that promise.
